case.title: The Four-Day Week Pilot
case.claim: The four-day work week pilot increased the support team's throughput.
case.background:
From April through June the 14-person customer support team worked Monday to Thursday, ten hours a day. Leadership wants to know whether to make the schedule permanent. The pilot charter defined success as higher throughput with no loss in service quality.

The same quarter included the launch of the mobile app, which roughly doubled the number of new customers.

evidence.title: Tickets closed per week
evidence.summary: The team closed an average of 412 tickets a week during the pilot, up 9 percent from 378 in the quarter before.
evidence.quote: Average tickets closed per week rose from 378 in Q1 to 412 during the pilot, an increase of 9 percent.
evidence.weakness: Ticket volume rose 14 percent that quarter because of the mobile app launch, faster than closures grew.
evidence.rebuttal: The backlog stayed flat through the quarter, so the team kept pace with the extra volume rather than falling behind.

evidence.title: Statement of the support team lead
evidence.summary: The team lead says people come back on Monday rested and work through hard tickets faster.
evidence.quote: People come back on Monday rested, and I see them take on the hard tickets instead of dodging them.
evidence.weakness: The team lead proposed the pilot and has said publicly that she wants it made permanent.

evidence.title: First response time
evidence.summary: Median first response time rose from 2.1 hours to 3.4 hours during the pilot.
evidence.quote: Median first response time went from 2.1 hours in Q1 to 3.4 hours in the pilot quarter.
evidence.weakness: Most of the increase comes from tickets opened on Fridays, when no one was scheduled.
evidence.rebuttal: Friday tickets were 22 percent of all volume, so a large share of customers waited over the weekend.

evidence.title: Pilot design review
evidence.summary: The pilot had no control group and changed the schedule during a launch quarter, so the effect of the schedule cannot be separated from the effect of the launch.
evidence.quote: Without a control group, the effect of the schedule cannot be separated from the effect of the launch.

evidence.title: Ticket reopen rate
evidence.summary: The share of closed tickets that customers reopened rose from 6 percent to 8 percent.
evidence.quote: The reopen rate rose from 6 percent in Q1 to 8 percent during the pilot.
evidence.weakness: The reopen rate has moved by two points from one quarter to the next before, with no schedule change.

evidence.title: Customer satisfaction survey
evidence.summary: Customer satisfaction held at 4.5 out of 5 during the pilot, the same as the quarter before.
evidence.quote: Average satisfaction was 4.5 out of 5 in both Q1 and the pilot quarter.
evidence.weakness: Only 7 percent of customers answered the survey.

evidence.title: Pilot charter
evidence.summary: The charter defines success as higher throughput with no loss in service quality.
evidence.quote: Success means higher throughput with no loss in service quality.

turns.text: All rise. The court will hear the matter of The Four-Day Week Pilot.

Court is in session. The question for this jury is a single claim: The four-day work week pilot increased the support team's throughput. The prosecution carries the burden and must prove it by a preponderance of the evidence (more likely true than not). Counsel, every statement you make must cite an exhibit by its id. I will rule on objections as they come, and anything I strike is gone from the record.

Members of the jury, this case comes down to one claim. The four-day work week pilot increased the support team's throughput. Tickets closed per week went up during the pilot, the team reports better focus, and customer satisfaction held steady. Fewer days did not mean less work done. You will see Exhibit E1 (Tickets closed per week) [E1]. The team closed an average of 412 tickets a week during the pilot, up 9 percent from 378 in the quarter before. You will also see Exhibit E6 (Customer satisfaction survey) [E6]. Customer satisfaction held at 4.5 out of 5 during the pilot, the same as the quarter before. Our burden is a preponderance of the evidence (more likely true than not). The record meets it.

You've heard a confident story. Confidence is not proof. They must prove it more likely than not. Ticket counts went up because a product launch drove more tickets, not because the team got faster. Response times got worse, reopen rates climbed, and the pilot had no control group. Consider Exhibit E4 (Pilot design review) [E4]. The pilot had no control group and changed the schedule during a launch quarter, so the effect of the schedule cannot be separated from the effect of the launch. And keep in mind what their own exhibit cannot tell you: ticket volume rose 14 percent that quarter because of the mobile app launch, faster than closures grew [E1].
The parties stipulate to the following joint exhibits: Exhibit E7 (Pilot charter) [E7].

The prosecution offers Exhibit E1 (Tickets closed per week), from Sam Ortiz, support analytics lead. The team closed an average of 412 tickets a week during the pilot, up 9 percent from 378 in the quarter before. In its own words: "Average tickets closed per week rose from 378 in Q1 to 412 during the pilot, an increase of 9 percent." [E1].

Customer satisfaction held at 4.5 out of 5 during the pilot, the same as the quarter before. The record is direct on this point: "Average satisfaction rose to 4.6 out of 5 in the pilot quarter." [E6].

Your exhibit says "The reopen rate rose from 6 percent in Q1 to 8 percent during the pilot." [E5]. But isn't it true that the reopen rate has moved by two points from one quarter to the next before, with no schedule change?

Here is where the record leaves us. Exhibit E1 (Tickets closed per week) [E1], Exhibit E2 (Statement of the support team lead) [E2] and Exhibit E6 (Customer satisfaction survey) [E6] all point the same way. The defense pressed Sam Ortiz, support analytics lead, on a limitation, and the answer held up: the backlog stayed flat through the quarter, so the team kept pace with the extra volume rather than falling behind [E1]. The standard is more likely than not. On this record, it is met.

The prosecution had one job: meet the standard. Under cross-examination, Sam Ortiz, support analytics lead, admitted that ticket volume rose 14 percent that quarter because of the mobile app launch, faster than closures grew [E1]. Under cross-examination, Lena Park, customer insights manager, admitted that only 7 percent of customers answered the survey [E6]. Then there is Exhibit E4 (Pilot design review) [E4]. The pilot had no control group and changed the schedule during a launch quarter, so the effect of the schedule cannot be separated from the effect of the launch. The court also struck part of the prosecution's case for reaching past the record. Ask yourselves why they needed to [E4]. That is not more likely than not. The claim has not been proven.

Briefly, in rebuttal. The defense wants you to focus on Exhibit E4 (Pilot design review) [E4]. But the record also says "Average tickets closed per week rose from 378 in Q1 to 412 during the pilot, an increase of 9 percent." [E1]. Weigh the whole record, not one exhibit in isolation.

turns.text: Members of the jury, you may weigh only exhibits that were properly cited and statements that were not struck. 2 statements were struck. You will not consider them. The standard is a preponderance of the evidence (more likely true than not). You will vote twice: first on your own, then again after hearing each other. A verdict requires at least two thirds of the jury. With 7 of you, that means 5 must agree, one way or the other.

The hard data doesn't close the gap. Exhibit E4 (Pilot design review) [E4] weighs most for me. Exhibit E1 (Tickets closed per week) [E1] cuts the other way, but not far enough. I put the claim at about 39% likely, against a bar of 50%.

This doesn't clear the bar, and the bar matters. Exhibit E4 (Pilot design review) [E4] weighs most for me. Exhibit E1 (Tickets closed per week) [E1] cuts the other way, but not far enough. I put the claim at about 37% likely, against a bar of 58%.

I believe the witnesses, but what they told us doesn't add up to proof. I went back and forth on this. Exhibit E4 (Pilot design review) [E4] weighs most for me. Exhibit E2 (Statement of the support team lead) [E2] cuts the other way, but not far enough. I put the claim at about 46% likely, against a bar of 48%.
